Honest answer: no — I wouldn't support it, at least not as the initiative proposes it.

The core problem is arithmetic. The fee is CHF 335, the initiative caps it at 200 — a cut of roughly 40%, something like CHF 600 million a year, or about a third of SRG's budget. That's not an amount you find through efficiency. It forces a choice: either SRG cuts deep into things only it provides (Romansh programming, the Italian-language service, regional studios, multilingual election coverage, emergency broadcasting), or the federal government fills the gap — which the media law arguably obliges it to do. The second option bothers me more: an SRG financed from the federal budget has to come back to parliament hat in hand every year, and that's precisely the setup that has corroded public broadcasters' independence elsewhere in Europe. The fee model, whatever its flaws, keeps the money at arm's length from politicians.

I'll grant the other side its best points, because they're real. CHF 200 isn't absurd in absolute terms — Austria's ORF levy is in that range. Households feel 335 as a burden, especially those who never switch on SRF. SRG holds reserves and is already under pressure to save. But a sudden constitutional cap with the mandate untouched doesn't even fix the fairness grievance — you'd still be forced to pay, just less — and hard-coding a price into the constitution with no inflation mechanism is bad design. Parliament has already trimmed the fee twice recently; that's the saner lever. If the real objection is compulsion, the coherent position was the 2018 No Billag initiative, not a cheaper Billag.

So: moderately confident no, resting ultimately on how much you value the four-language mandate. And since you're arguing the other side anyway — you've got decent cards (reserves, the ORF comparison, the flat levy's regressivity). Happy to help you build that case if useful.
